# Text Mining

## Set Up

```{r}
library(readr)
pubmed <- read_csv("pubmed.csv")
```

## Question 1

How many abstracts are associated with each search term? Tokenize the abstracts and count the number of each token. Do you see anything interesting? What are the 5 most common tokens for each search term?

### Summary

- The five most common tokens showed a similar pattern across the different search terms, with general scientific and biomedical vocabulary appearing frequently. While some topic-specific terminology was present, common stop words made up a large portion of the most frequent tokens.

```{r}
# Abstract Counts
library(tidyverse)

abstract_counts <-
  pubmed %>%
  count(term, sort = TRUE)

abstract_counts

# Tokenize abstracts
library(tidytext)

tokens <-
  pubmed %>%
  select(term, abstract) %>%
  unnest_tokens(word, abstract)

tokens

# Count all terms
token_counts <-
  tokens %>%
  count(term, word, sort = TRUE)

token_counts

# Top 5 tokens for each term
top5_tokens <-
  token_counts %>%
  group_by(term) %>%
  slice_max(n, n = 5) %>%
  arrange(term, desc(n))

top5_tokens

# Top 5 tokens visualization 
top5_tokens %>%
  mutate(word = reorder_within(word, n, term)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(n, word, fill = term)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~term, scales = "free") +
  scale_y_reordered() +
  labs(
    title = "Five Most Common Tokens by Search Term",
    x = "Count",
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Question 2

Does removing stop words change what tokens appear as the most frequent? What are the 5 most common tokens for each search term after removing stop words?

### Summary

- After removing the stop words, the disease-specific terminology become much more visible. Instead of generic English words dominating the rankings, medically relevant terms associated with each search topic emerge as the most frequent tokens.

```{r}
# Remove the stop words
tidy_no_stop <-
  tokens %>%
  anti_join(stop_words, by = c("word"))

# Top 5 words after removing stop words 
top5_no_stop <-
  tidy_no_stop %>%
  count(term, word, sort = TRUE) %>%
  group_by(term) %>%
  slice_max(n, n = 5)

top5_no_stop

# Updated top 5 tokens visualization 
top5_no_stop %>%
  mutate(word = reorder_within(word, n, term)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(n, word, fill = term)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~term, scales = "free") +
  scale_y_reordered() +
  labs(
    title = "Top Tokens After Stop Word Removal",
    x = "Count",
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Question 3

Tokenize the abstracts into bigrams. Find the 10 most common bigrams and visualize them. - Common English stop words were removed prior to calculating bigram frequencies to improve interpretation of the resulting word pairs.

```{r}
# Create and clean Bigrams
bigrams <-
  pubmed %>%
  unnest_tokens(
    bigram,
    abstract,
    token = "ngrams",
    n = 2
  ) %>%
  separate(
    bigram,
    into = c("word1", "word2"),
    sep = " "
  ) %>%
  filter(
    !word1 %in% stop_words$word,
    !word2 %in% stop_words$word
  ) %>%
  unite(
    bigram,
    word1,
    word2,
    sep = " "
  )

head(bigrams)

# Count Bigrams
bigram_counts <-
  bigrams %>%
  count(
    bigram,
    sort = TRUE
  )

head(bigram_counts)

# Identify the most common Bigrams
top10_bigrams <-
  bigram_counts %>%
  slice_max(
    n,
    n = 10
  )

top10_bigrams

# Top 10 Bigrams Visualization 
top10_bigrams %>%
  mutate(
    bigram = reorder(
      bigram,
      n
    )
  ) %>%
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = n,
      y = bigram
    )
  ) +
  geom_col(
    fill = "steelblue"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Top 10 Most Common Bigrams",
    x = "Count",
    y = "Bigram"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Question 4

Calculate the TF-IDF value for each word-search term combination (here you want the search term to be the “document”). What are the 5 tokens from each search term with the highest TF-IDF value? How are the results different from the answers you got in Question 1?

### Summary

- The TF-IDF results differ from Question 1 because they highlight terms that are more distinctive and relevant to each search topic rather than simply identifying the most frequently occurring words. In Question 1, common scientific terms and general biomedical vocabulary appeared frequently across the abstracts. However, TF-IDF gives greater importance to words that are more specific to a particular topic and less common across the overall collection of abstracts.

```{r}
# Count words in each term 
word_counts <-
  tidy_no_stop %>%
  count(term, word)

# Calculate TF-IDF 
tfidf_tbl <-
  word_counts %>%
  bind_tf_idf(
    word,
    term,
    n
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(tf_idf))

tfidf_tbl

# Top 5 terms per topic
top_tfidf <-
  tfidf_tbl %>%
  group_by(term) %>%
  slice_max(tf_idf, n = 5)

top_tfidf

# Top TF-IDF Visualization 
top_tfidf %>%
  mutate(
    word =
      reorder_within(
        word,
        tf_idf,
        term
      )
  ) %>%
  ggplot(
    aes(
      tf_idf,
      word,
      fill = term
    )
  ) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~term, scales = "free") +
  scale_y_reordered() +
  labs(
    title = "Top TF-IDF Terms by Search Topic",
    x = "TF-IDF",
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

# Sentiment Analysis

## Question 5

Perform a sentiment analysis using the NRC lexicon. What is the most common sentiment for each search term? What if you remove "positive" and "negative" from the list?

### Summary

- When positive and negative sentiments were included, they accounted for the highest counts across most search topics. However, after removing them, more specific emotional patterns became visible. Fear was the most common remaining sentiment for COVID, meningitis, and prostate cancer, while disgust was most common for cystic fibrosis and anticipation was most common for preeclampsia.

```{r}
# Load NRC 
nrc <- get_sentiments("nrc")

# Join sentiment labels
nrc_sentiment <-
  tidy_no_stop %>%
  inner_join(
    nrc,
    by = c("word")
  )

# Count sentiments
sentiment_counts <-
  nrc_sentiment %>%
  count(
    term,
    sentiment,
    sort = TRUE
  )

sentiment_counts

# Common sentiments per term
sentiment_counts %>%
  group_by(term) %>%
  slice_max(n, n = 1)

# Most Common sentiment Plot
sentiment_counts %>%
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = sentiment,
      y = n,
      fill = term
    )
  ) +
  geom_col() +
  facet_wrap(~term) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "NRC Sentiment Counts by Search Term",
    x = "Sentiment",
    y = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

# Remove Positive & Negative
sentiment_no_pn <-
  nrc_sentiment %>%
  filter(
    !sentiment %in% c(
      "positive",
      "negative"
    )
  )

# Count remaining sentiments
sentiment_no_pn_counts <-
  sentiment_no_pn %>%
  count(
    term,
    sentiment,
    sort = TRUE
  )

sentiment_no_pn_counts

# Most common sentiments w/o + or -
sentiment_no_pn_counts %>%
  group_by(term) %>%
  slice_max(
    n,
    n = 1
  )

# Sentiments w/o + or - Plot
sentiment_no_pn_counts %>%
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = sentiment,
      y = n,
      fill = term
    )
  ) +
  geom_col() +
  facet_wrap(~term) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "NRC Sentiments by Search Term (Excluding Positive and Negative)",
    x = "Sentiment",
    y = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Question 6

Perform a sentiment analysis using the AFINN lexicon to get an average positivity score for each abstract (hint: you may want to create a variable that indexes, or counts, the abstracts). Create a visualization that shows these scores grouped by search term. Are any search terms noticeably different from the others?

### Summary

- Yes, these terms are noticeably different. Cystic fibrosis stands out because it has the highest median sentiment score, which is slightly positive compared with the other search terms, whose median scores are slightly negative. Prostate cancer also has a noticeably narrower distribution, suggesting less variation in sentiment scores across its abstracts.

```{r}
# Create unique abstract IDs
unique_pubmed <-
  pubmed %>%
  mutate(
    abstract_id = row_number()
  )

# Tokenize abstracts
afinn_tokens <-
  unique_pubmed %>%
  unnest_tokens(
    word,
    abstract
  )

# Join AFFIN lexicon
afinn_scores <-
  afinn_tokens %>%
  inner_join(
    get_sentiments("afinn"),
    by = c("word")
  )

# Calculate AVG sentiment score per abstract
abstract_sentiment <-
  afinn_scores %>%
  group_by(
    abstract_id,
    term
  ) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_score = mean(value),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# AFINN Sentiment Visualization 
ggplot(
  abstract_sentiment,
  aes(
    x = term,
    y = mean_score,
    fill = term
  )
) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    title = "Average AFINN Sentiment Score by Search Term",
    x = "Search Term",
    y = "Average Sentiment Score"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none"
  )
```
